name: Bayberry & wax myrtle
why: Blocked by three independent safety reviewers across three revision rounds. Each reviewer approved of the entry's central thesis and each found new safety-critical gaps, so the defect rate was not converging. Under the rule this corpus runs on — nothing publishes without an independent confirm pass — it stays out.
unresolved: Sweet gale (Myrica gale) clears every leaf-in-hand test bayberry has. Three attempts to exclude it by rule failed. It is aromatic, alternate, resin-dotted, leathery and multi-stemmed, it grows on firm sandy pond margins and shore swales as well as peat, and on a fruitless shrub in July there may be nothing in the hand that separates the two. The third reviewer's proposed fix is to stop treating pond edges, swale bottoms, bog margins and salt-marsh rims as picking ground at all.

Ngaio (Myoporum laetum) on the West Coast defeats the single confirmatory character: it has visible gland dots. Planted by the mile as a California coastal hedge, hepatotoxic, and it passes five of the six checks.
Poison sumac was missing, on ground the entry sends readers to.
note: The third reviewer claimed the guide treats poison sumac as a mandatory lookalike in every entry touching wet ground. That is not true — it is named in elderberry, staghorn sumac and wild blueberry, which are the three entries where it is actually confusable. The claim was overstated; the underlying finding about this entry was not.

entry.name: Bayberry & wax myrtle
entry.scientific: Morella pensylvanica and M. cerifera; also M. caroliniensis (evergreen bayberry) in the southeastern coastal plain and M. californica (Pacific wax myrtle) on the West Coast. All four were long placed in Myrica, and USDA PLANTS, older field guides and most nursery labels still say Myrica pensylvanica, M. cerifera and M. californica — same plants. Two names in the neighbourhood are not the same plant: Morella inodora, the scentless bayberry of the northern Gulf, and Myrica gale (sweet gale), a separate genus that is aromatic but not interchangeable. See lookalikes for both.
entry.habitat:
Acid, low-nutrient, usually sandy ground in full sun, nearly always within reach of the coast. It fixes its own nitrogen in root nodules, so it colonises bare sterile sand where almost nothing else will: a dense dark-green shrub island on an otherwise open sand flat is very often this plant. In the Northeast that means back-dune thickets and the damp swales behind the primary dune, the upland margins of salt marshes, pine barrens, pond and bog edges and abandoned sandy fields, in company with pitch pine, eastern red cedar, beach plum, black cherry, bearberry, greenbrier and a great deal of shrubby poison ivy — and note that three of those companions are on the lookalike list below. Northern bayberry runs from the Maritimes south to North Carolina; scattered inland and Great Lakes populations are tracked as rare in some states and are not a foraging resource, so leave them. Southern wax myrtle takes over from roughly southern New Jersey south through Florida and west to eastern Texas and central Arkansas, on pond and swamp margins, pocosin rims, pine flatwoods and wet prairies, but also on dry sandhills and hard along roadsides and fencerows. M. caroliniensis fills the wetter southeastern coastal plain between the two. Pacific wax myrtle holds the fog belt from Grays Harbor, Washington to southern California, on coastal bluffs, dune scrub, canyon bottoms and moist wooded slopes.

Two facts about this ground do most of the safety work. First, most of the plants you can actually reach in the Southeast and on the West Coast are nursery stock in clipped hedges, standing shoulder to shoulder with oleander, cherry laurel, Florida anise, Pieris and privet — which is to say, beside most of the things here that can hurt you. Second, where a dune swale or pond edge grades into saturated peat you have left bayberry ground and entered sweet gale, bog laurel and Labrador tea ground, and two of those three are aromatic.
entry.indicator: The gray-green shrub band immediately behind the primary dune, where beach grass gives out and pitch pine and eastern red cedar begin — or, in the Southeast, the wax myrtle rim of a pond-pine pocosin or a wet longleaf flatwoods. Because it makes its own nitrogen, it is usually the greenest thing standing on the poorest sand.
entry.parts:
The leaves, and only the leaves — used like a bay leaf: dried, simmered whole in stock, beans, braises, chowder and pickling brine, then fished out before the pot reaches the table. They are alternate along the twig, simple, leathery, 1.5–4 in long, widest above the middle and tapering to a narrow wedge at the base, dull to glossy dark green above and paler beneath. Two things are constant across all four species: the RESIN DOTS, sunken golden to orange-brown glands scattered across the underside (and on both faces in wax myrtle), visible held to the light and gritty under a thumbnail; and the SCENT, which on a hard crush is sweet resinous balsam and candle wax, closer to bay rum than to a Mediterranean bay leaf.

MARGINS ARE NOT A TEST, IN EITHER DIRECTION. Northern bayberry is usually entire or carries a few blunt teeth on the upper third; southern and Pacific wax myrtle are often distinctly serrate along much of the upper half. So teeth cannot confirm a bayberry for you, and they cannot reject hollyleaf cherry, toyon or chokecherry for you either. Earlier versions of this entry used teeth as a test. They were wrong to, and no teeth clause survives below.

THE POT IS THE DOSE, AND TAKING THE LEAF OUT IS NOT A SAFETY STEP. This is the most important paragraph here. Every deadly plant below poisons through the BROTH, not through the leaf you fish out. Cyanogenic glycosides (prunasin and amygdalin — the cherry laurels, the deciduous cherries and plums, hollyleaf cherry, toyon) are water-soluble: some hydrogen cyanide boils off an open pot, but the intact glycoside stays in the stock and is cleaved to cyanide by your own gut bacteria after you drink it. 'Laurel water', an infusion of exactly these leaves, was a historical murder weapon. Cardiac glycosides (oleandrin, neriine — oleander) are heat-stable and water-soluble, and the documented deaths are from leaf TEA: the flavour the plant left behind after the plant itself was taken out. Grayanotoxins (the laurels, Pieris, Lyonia, Leucothoe, the Labrador teas) are non-volatile, heat-stable and water-soluble — as this guide already says under sassafras and wild blueberry, they survive wilting, drying, grinding and the gumbo pot, and heated mad honey stays toxic. Anisatin (Illicium) is extracted by hot water; every star-anise seizure case in the literature is an infusion. And urushiol, from the poison ivy and poison oak growing up through this thicket at exactly the height you are reaching, is not destroyed by heat or by drying either — a single leaflet boiled in a stock puts urushiol in the food, not just on your hands. A 20–30 minute simmer is not a decontamination step. It is an extraction step.

SO: IF A LEAF YOU CANNOT NAME WENT INTO THE POT, THROW OUT THE POT. Not the leaf — the stock, the beans, the braise, the brine, and anything already ladled out of it. Do not skim it, do not dilute it, do not taste a spoonful to see. Count the leaves in and count them out if you like, but understand that the count is a CHOKING control, not a poison control. If anyone has eaten and there is any doubt about what went in, call Poison Control on 1-800-222-1222 immediately rather than waiting for symptoms.

THE CHECK. Run it on every leaf, one at a time, on the plant and again on the drying screen — once leaves are dried and mixed, the evidence of what went in is gone and every hazard here is still fully potent. Six lines. Each one can only REJECT. None of them says yes on its own, and a leaf has to clear all six.

1. SNAP IT OFF. Milky white sap, or leaves in opposite pairs or whorls along the twig — STOP. (Oleander, privet, Carolina jessamine, sheep and bog laurel.)
2. UNDERSIDE TO THE LIGHT. No field of small sunken golden-orange dots in a flat green surface, gritty under a thumbnail — STOP. Anything that rubs off under a thumb, rusty wool or scales or a white bloom — STOP. A vein running parallel just inside the margin all the way round — STOP. Two or three swellings where the main veins fork, instead of a scattered field of dots — STOP. (Nearly everything below fails this line.)
3. PETIOLE AND LEAF BASE. Any raised bump or gland where the blade meets the stalk, or on either side of the midrib near the base — STOP. (Every Prunus: cherry laurel, chokecherry, black cherry, beach plum, hollyleaf cherry.)
4. BEND IT. A thin, soft blade that folds and tears like a garden leaf — STOP. Bayberry is leathery and stiff and springs back. (This is the line that catches the deciduous cherries and plums, which are in leaf in exactly the months this entry sends you out in.) Very new growth is soft on any shrub; leave it and take mature leaves, so this line means what it says.
5. CRUSH HARD AND SAY WHAT YOU SMELL, OUT LOUD. Almond, marzipan or maraschino — STOP. Anise or licorice — STOP. Camphor or eucalyptus — STOP. Turpentine or sharp medicinal — STOP. Nothing at all — STOP. Only sweet balsam and candle wax goes on. 'It smelled nice' is not this line; cherry laurel, Illicium and Labrador tea all smell wonderful.
6. LOOK AT YOUR FEET, AND AROUND YOU. Peat that squelches, standing water, or a clipped hedge, roadside verge, median or foundation bed — STOP, whatever the leaf says.

WHAT THE CHECK CANNOT SETTLE: SWEET GALE. A leaf can clear all six lines and still be Myrica gale, and you should stop expecting a clause to fix that. Sweet gale is in this same family. It is alternate, genuinely resin-dotted, bleeds no latex, carries no petiole glands and no intramarginal vein, grows as a multi-stemmed shrub and smells sweet and resinous on a crush. Every separator that gets published fails exactly where you need it: the shrubs are dioecious, so on a male plant there is no fruit to compare with a gray wax berry; both species can be entire-margined, so 'teeth at the tip versus teeth along the upper half' resolves nothing and is finer than anyone can work in the field anyway; the leaves overlap in size; and 'sand that drains, not peat' is contradicted by this entry's own habitat text, which sends you to pond edges, damp swales, salt-marsh margins and swamp rims. On a fruitless shrub at a pond edge in July there may be nothing in your hand that tells the two apart. That is the honest state of it, and a rule that resolves it on paper would be a lie.

So take the consequence instead of a false pass. Line 6 is the operative rule and it rejects on location, not on the leaf: at the peat seam, don't pick — not because the leaf is unreadable but because that seam is where three different aromatic shrubs stand and two of them, bog laurel and Labrador tea, are graded deadly here. Pick where the ground is firm sand and you are not at that seam at all.

And know the size of this particular mistake, because it is not the size of the others. Sweet gale is a seasoning and beer-bittering herb in northern Europe. A leaf of it in a stock is not a poisoning emergency and does not on its own mean throwing out the pot. What it does mean is this: the plant is a listed abortifacient, contraindicated in pregnancy, and its essential oil is toxic in quantity (the seed oil should never be ingested). So do not serve a pot you suspect to anyone pregnant or trying to conceive, do not use it in quantity, and do not make it a routine. That is the true warning. Grading it as poison would not be.

THE SEASON, AND WHO IT PROTECTS. In the Northeast, run all of this between June and September and not outside it. From about November to April northern bayberry is bare or down to a few tired semi-evergreen leaves while cherry laurel, mountain laurel, dog-hobble, Lyonia, Pieris, bog laurel, Labrador tea and Illicium are every one of them in full glossy leaf, so a leathery evergreen leaf off a northeastern dune thicket in winter is more likely to be one of them than bayberry. That is why the guide does not list this species for a northeastern reader outside the summer window. BUT THE MONTH RESTRICTION PROTECTS THE NORTHEAST AND NOWHERE ELSE, and if you are anywhere else you must not read it as a safety window applied on your behalf. In the Southeast, South Central and West every deadly lookalike on this list is evergreen and fully present in June through September — cherry laurel, Illicium, Pieris, Carolina jessamine, camphor tree, hollyleaf cherry, toyon and the western heaths. Southern and Pacific wax myrtle are themselves evergreen and pickable year-round in their own ranges. The calendar does nothing for you there. The six lines do.

STRENGTH AND HANDLING. Northern bayberry is milder than Laurus nobilis, so use roughly twice as many leaves — two where a recipe calls for one. Wax myrtle is near enough to bay to swap one for one. Pacific wax myrtle is the least documented of the four in a kitchen; start with one leaf. Drying 10–14 days in a paper bag concentrates the aroma and takes off a grassy edge. Simmer at least 20–30 minutes to get anything out of a leaf.

Never eat the leaf itself: like a bay leaf it stays stiff and sharp-edged through any amount of cooking, and swallowed whole leaves of this kind have caused choking and tears to the throat and gut. Do not drink the leaves as a strong daily tea or take them as a concentrated extract — the aromatic resin is a flavouring dose, not a medicinal one, and concentrated bayberry preparations should be avoided in pregnancy. The gray waxy fruit is candle and soap stock, not food. Leave the root bark entirely alone: it is a traditional emetic, strongly nauseating in quantity, and bayberry bark tannin has been reported as tumour-inducing in rodent feeding studies. Bayberry leaf needs no leaching or boiling to be made safe — but that is a statement about bayberry and about nothing else in your basket, and it is the sentence a reader is most likely to over-read. The safety of the dish rests on what you put in, never on what you take out.

lookalikes.name: Cherry laurel — Carolina laurelcherry (Prunus caroliniana) and the planted and escaped English cherry laurel (P. laurocerasus)
lookalikes.tell: THIS IS THE ONE THAT KILLS PEOPLE LOOKING FOR A WILD BAY LEAF, AND IT DEFEATS THE SMELL TEST AS NORMALLY TAUGHT. A crushed cherry laurel leaf is strongly and pleasantly aromatic — marzipan, almond extract, maraschino — because bruising it releases hydrogen cyanide. 'It smelled good when I crushed it' is therefore not an identification, which is why line 5 asks you to name the smell rather than rate it. Leaf tells that work on a picked green leaf in any month: thicker, glossier and darker than bayberry, broadest near the apex, with a few sharp bristle-tipped teeth (upper leaves often entire), NO resin dots anywhere on the underside, and extrafloral nectaries — two or more small raised dark glands on the petiole or beside the midrib near the base, which no Morella has. It grows into a single-trunked tree to 30–40 ft with smooth gray bark; bayberry stays a multi-stemmed shrub. Snap a twig: cherry laurel wood smells of almond, bayberry of resin. Leaves run 1–2.5% cyanogenic glycosides, around 3.3 g prunasin equivalents per 100 g fresh. Wilting is what makes the foliage most dangerous as browse; fully dried leaves lose free HCN over time, but the intact glycoside — the part that matters once it is in a broth — stays, comes out into the stock in the first minutes of a simmer and is cleaved to cyanide in your gut after the leaf is long gone. Italy recorded 147 cherry laurel intoxications between 1995 and 2007 and 28 more in 2015, largely from confusion with culinary bay; 31 sheep in Scotland and 36 cattle in Ireland died on hedge clippings. P. caroliniana is native through the southeastern coastal plain and planted everywhere as hedge, routinely next to landscape wax myrtle; P. laurocerasus is a standard northeastern hedge shrub and is invasive in the Pacific Northwest, inside Pacific wax myrtle's range. Cyanide poisoning is fast — headache, dizziness, gasping, dilated pupils, weakness, convulsions, collapse. Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) immediately.

lookalikes.name: The soft-leaved cherries and plums of the summer thicket — chokecherry (Prunus virginiana), black cherry (P. serotina) and beach plum (P. maritima)
lookalikes.tell: THE HAZARD THAT IS PRESENT ONLY IN THE MONTHS THIS ENTRY SENDS YOU OUT IN, AND THE HABITAT PARAGRAPH ABOVE NAMES TWO OF THEM AS BAYBERRY'S OWN COMPANIONS. Every other deadly plant here is evergreen, and the entry's seasonal argument is built entirely around evergreens — so understand that it does not cover these three at all. They are in full leaf in June through September, standing in the same back-dune thicket, the same old field, the same fencerow. Chokecherry is the worst of them for shape: a multi-stemmed shrub with alternate, simple, obovate leaves widest above the middle, which is the exact outline this entry gives for bayberry. Black cherry is narrower and glossier with incurved blunt teeth and, on the underside, a dense band of rusty-orange hairs along the midrib. Beach plum is a dune shrub with dull, finely toothed leaves, hairy beneath, growing where northeastern bayberry grows. FOUR TELLS, ALL OF THEM IN THE CHECK ABOVE. (1) No resin dots: the underside is a plain surface, and a thumbnail finds nothing gritty. (2) Raised glands on the petiole or at the base of the blade — one or two small bumps — which no Morella has. (3) The blade is THIN and soft; it folds and tears like a garden leaf where a bayberry leaf is leathery and springs back. This is the one to lean on in summer, because it separates them at arm's length. (4) Snap a twig and smell it: bitter almond, not resin. All three carry prunasin and amygdalin. Wilting is what makes the foliage most dangerous as browse and has killed a great deal of livestock; drying loses free HCN slowly, but the glycoside survives drying and a 20–30 minute simmer extracts it straight into the stock, where your own gut flora finish the job. Cyanide poisoning is fast. Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) immediately.

lookalikes.name: The California evergreen cherries and toyon — hollyleaf cherry (Prunus ilicifolia), Catalina cherry (P. lyonii) and toyon (Heteromeles arbutifolia)
lookalikes.tell: THE WEST COAST'S CHERRY LAUREL. Hollyleaf cherry is the leathery, alternate, evergreen, spiny-toothed shrub of coastal California bluffs, canyon bottoms, dune scrub and chaparral — Morella californica's own ground, Bay Area south into Baja. Catalina cherry is the island form with larger, mostly entire, flatter leaves, planted throughout coastal southern California and naturalised from those plantings; the two hybridise freely, so margins on a garden plant tell you nothing. Toyon is the third leathery serrate evergreen on the same bluff and carries the same chemistry. WHAT SEPARATES ALL THREE FROM PACIFIC WAX MYRTLE. (1) NO RESIN DOTS — turn the leaf over against the light and the underside is plain, with nothing sunken in it and nothing gritty under a thumbnail. Morella californica has a field of sunken golden-orange glands on both faces. (2) THE TEETH BITE: hollyleaf cherry and toyon teeth are hard and spine-tipped and prick a finger drawn along the margin, and hollyleaf cherry's blade is stiff and often cupped. Wax myrtle's serrations are soft and flat. (3) THE CRUSH: Prunus gives almond or nothing, toyon a bitter green nothing, wax myrtle sweet balsam and candle wax. Snap a twig — Prunus wood smells of bitter almond. (4) GLANDS on the petiole or leaf base of both cherries, which no Morella has. Fruit ends it: a single dark stone fruit on the cherries, clusters of bright red pomes on toyon, never a bumpy gray wax ball. Both cherries carry prunasin and amygdalin; toyon's cyanogenic glycosides run through leaves and immature fruit, highest in new growth, and have killed horses off browse — the published toyon levels are lower and less consistent than the cherries', which is a reason to reject it, not a margin to work in. The hazard stays in the broth after the leaf is out. Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222).

lookalikes.name: Oleander (Nerium oleander)
lookalikes.tell: Line 1 of the check settles this one in a single look, and it is worth making that look a habit: oleander leaves are OPPOSITE or in whorls of three, bayberry leaves are strictly alternate. Oleander's are long, narrow, stiff and leathery, uniformly dark green, perfectly entire, with a conspicuous pale midrib and fine parallel side veins; there are no resin dots and no scent on a hard crush. Break a leaf or stem and it bleeds sticky white latex — bayberry never does, in any species or season. This matters because oleander is planted by the thousand along Gulf and South Atlantic roads, medians, parking lots and old homesites, has escaped in the Deep South, and is among the commonest landscape shrubs in coastal California: the same disturbed coastal ground where wax myrtle is planted and volunteers, at the same height and habit. Every part carries cardiac glycosides (oleandrin, neriine) at a concentration where a single leaf is a plausible lethal dose for a child. The documented cooking-adjacent route is the one that matters here and it is a broth route: deaths from leaves brewed as TEA. Oleandrin is heat-stable and water-soluble, so taking the leaf out of the pot removes nothing. If oleander went into a pot, throw out everything in it and call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222). Nothing with milky sap and paired leaves goes in a stockpot, ever.

lookalikes.name: The grayanotoxin heaths, east and west — mountain, sheep and bog laurel (Kalmia latifolia, K. angustifolia, K. polifolia) and western bog laurel (K. microphylla); Pieris japonica and climbing fetterbush (P. phillyreifolia); fetterbush and staggerbush (Lyonia lucida, L. mariana, L. ferruginea); coastal dog-hobble (Leucothoe axillaris) and Sierra laurel (L. davisiae); Pacific rhododendron (Rhododendron macrophyllum) and swamp azalea (R. viscosum)
lookalikes.tell:
TREAT THIS AS A CHEMISTRY, NOT A CENSUS. The heath family runs to hundreds of leathery evergreen species and this list is a sample of the ones that physically grow interlaced with bayberry; absence of a name from it is not absence from the thicket. Lines 2 and 5 of the check reject the whole family whether or not a species is named here, and that is the protection — not the roll-call. EAST: Kalmia angustifolia is in 'moist bogs, swamps, disturbed areas, roadsides, and dry pine forests' across the Northeast, which is northern bayberry ground, sand and peat alike; Lyonia and Leucothoe axillaris build the southeastern pocosin and flatwoods thickets that wax myrtle rims; bog laurel stands in the peat seam at the sweet gale boundary. Pieris japonica is not wild but is one of the most heavily planted leathery evergreen hedge shrubs in both the Northeast and the Southeast, and stands in exactly the clipped-hedge row this entry names as its main practical risk; P. phillyreifolia is native to southeastern bays and pocosins and climbs inside the bark of pond cypress. WEST: Rhododendron macrophyllum is the dominant leathery evergreen understory shrub of the coastal Pacific Northwest, squarely inside Morella californica's bluffs, canyon bottoms and moist wooded slopes, with large thick entire leaves whorled at the shoot tip; Kalmia microphylla holds coastal and montane peat with small opposite rolled-margin leaves, white beneath; Leucothoe davisiae holds Sierra and Cascade wet meadows and bogs with alternate leathery finely toothed leaves.

DO NOT USE LEAF ARRANGEMENT ON THIS GROUP. It is the tell most often published for it and it clears nothing. NC State gives Kalmia latifolia as 'simple, alternate… occasionally opposite or whorled' and Leucothoe axillaris flatly as ALTERNATE; every Lyonia is alternate, and Pieris is alternate but crowded into whorl-like rosettes. Only sheep laurel, bog laurel and western bog laurel are reliably opposite. An alternate-leaved mountain laurel passes an arrangement check cleanly, which would leave a beginner holding a deadly leaf with one test 'passed'.

WHAT ACTUALLY WORKS, AND YOU NEED BOTH. (1) THE UNDERSIDE held to the light. Morella carries sunken golden to orange-brown resin dots in a flat green surface, gritty under a thumbnail. None of these does: K. latifolia is plain pale yellow-green; K. polifolia and K. microphylla are white-glaucous with margins rolled strongly under; Lyonia ferruginea is coated in rusty-brown scales, not clear golden dots; Lyonia lucida — the closest match at arm's length, being alternate, glossy, leathery, evergreen and on the same wet acid ground — carries a conspicuous vein running parallel just inside the margin the whole way round, which no Morella has; Pieris and R. macrophyllum are plain beneath. (2) THE CRUSH. Thumbnail hard through the blade: these give you nothing at all, where bayberry gives sweet balsam and candle wax.

All of them carry grayanotoxin, concentrated in the LEAF, so a leaf simmered in a pot is the dangerous form. Grayanotoxins are non-volatile, heat-stable and water-soluble: they come out into the liquid and stay in the broth after the leaf is lifted out, exactly as they survive into heated mad honey and into dried laurel baled in hay. Salivation, vomiting, slowed heart, falling blood pressure, tingling, loss of coordination, seizures, paralysis, heart failure.

The working rule, and note which way it runs: IF A LEATHERY LEAF GIVES YOU NOTHING ON A HARD CRUSH, PUT IT DOWN, whatever else it looks like. That is a rejection only. It does not run backwards — cherry laurel, Illicium and the Labrador teas all smell wonderful.

lookalikes.name: The Labrador teas — bog Labrador tea (Rhododendron groenlandicum, syn. Ledum groenlandicum) and western or trapper's tea (R. columbianum, syn. Ledum glandulosum)
lookalikes.tell: THE PLANT THAT DEFEATS A POSITIVE AROMA RULE THE WAY CHERRY LAUREL DEFEATS A NEGATIVE ONE, and it stands in the exact peat seam line 6 of the check tells you to walk away from — where a dune swale or pond edge grades into saturated ground in the Northeast and around the Great Lakes, and in Pacific Northwest bogs and wet meadows inside Morella californica's range. These are ALTERNATE, leathery, entire evergreen heaths, 1–5 ft, strongly and pleasantly aromatic on a crush — resinous, camphoraceous, turpentine-and-tea — so a reader who learned 'no smell means put it down' will read the smell as confirmation. It confirms nothing. THE UNDERSIDE SETTLES IT IN ONE LOOK. R. groenlandicum has margins rolled strongly under and the whole lower surface felted in dense RUSTY-ORANGE WOOL you can rub into a visible fuzz with a thumb — a continuous mat of hair, not discrete sunken dots in a green surface. R. columbianum is less woolly but carries scattered stalked glands and fine hairs, and the margins still roll. A Morella underside is flat green with glandular pits sunk into it; rub it and nothing comes off. The leaves are also narrower and strap-like, 1–2.5 in, crowded at the shoot tips rather than spaced along the twig, and the fruit is a small dry capsule, never a gray wax ball. R. columbianum carries GRAYANOTOXIN and is the poisonous one of the pair; both carry ledol, and the standard caution on the genus is that the tea must not be steeped long or drunk daily. The ethnobotanical use of R. groenlandicum as a short-steeped beverage is real but is not licence here: the two are not reliably separable by a beginner, a 20–30 minute stock simmer is nothing like a short steep, and bog laurel stands in the same peat with similarly narrow rolled-margin leaves that are WHITE-glaucous rather than rusty beneath.

lookalikes.name: Carolina jessamine / yellow jessamine (Gelsemium sempervirens)
lookalikes.tell: Deadly, evergreen, leathery, and it drapes through exactly the southeastern fencerows, hedges, roadside thickets and pine-flatwoods edges where most of the accessible wax myrtle actually stands — often physically through the shrub, so a leaf can come off in your hand while you think you are picking bayberry. Two tells and both are in the check. It is a twining VINE, not a shrub: follow the stem and it wraps something. Its leaves are OPPOSITE, entire, lanceolate, shiny dark green, 1–3 in, with no resin dots and nothing at all on a hard crush. Yellow trumpet flowers in late winter and early spring make it obvious then and tell you nothing in July. Every part carries gelsemine and related alkaloids; the documented human fatalities include people who drank it as a TEA in mistake for honeysuckle, which is this entry's broth thesis in another plant. Weakness, dilated pupils, jaw and throat rigidity, difficulty breathing, convulsions, respiratory failure. Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222).

lookalikes.name: Florida anise and yellow anise / swamp star anise (Illicium floridanum, I. parviflorum)
lookalikes.tell: THE SOUTHEAST'S AROMATIC-CRUSH-POSITIVE HAZARD, and it occupies both of this entry's highest-risk situations at once. In the wild it holds streamhead bogs, bayheads, ravine bottoms and bay-forest rims across the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana and Georgia — the same ground as Morella inodora and the wax myrtle pocosin rim. In the landscape it is one of the most heavily planted evergreen shrubs in the Southeast, standing in hedges and foundation beds beside landscape wax myrtle. At a glance the leaves read as bayberry: alternate (though crowded into a pseudo-whorl at the shoot tip), simple, thick, leathery, glossy above and paler below, 2–6 in, on a multi-stemmed shrub, and STRONGLY AROMATIC when bruised — anise, licorice, what NC State's toolbox calls a gin-and-tonic smell. THREE TELLS. (1) SCENT IDENTITY, which is the whole reason line 5 asks for a specific smell and not for 'aromatic': anise is not sweet balsam and candle wax. The moment you get anise, you stop. (2) NO RESIN DOTS — the aroma is oil through the tissue, not glands, and the underside is plain with nothing gritty under a thumbnail. (3) Margins entire and often wavy, on a reddish-purple leaf stalk in I. floridanum, leaves in rosettes at the branch ends. The fruit is a flat many-pointed star. The genus makes anisatin and relatives, potent GABA antagonists; the Japanese star anise cases are the reference point — seven infants at one Florida hospital with seizures, jitteriness, vomiting, nystagmus and myoclonus after home-brewed star anise tea. Reported anisatin content in the two American species is lower and genuinely disputed, and NC State rates both poison severity LOW while still listing leaves, fruit and seeds as poisonous. Treat the dispute as a reason to keep it out of the pot, not a margin to work in: the toxin is heat-stable and water-extracted, and a 20–30 minute simmer is an infusion.

lookalikes.name: Sweet gale / bog myrtle (Myrica gale)
lookalikes.tell: THE ONE THE CHECK CANNOT SETTLE, AND THE ONE THIS ENTRY HAS STOPPED PRETENDING TO SETTLE. Read the sweet gale paragraph in the parts section with this. It is in the same family as bayberry and genuinely aromatic, resin-dotted, alternate, latex-free, gland-free, without an intramarginal vein, multi-stemmed — so it clears every line of the check except line 6. The separators you will find published do not work when you need them: the shrubs are dioecious, so a male plant offers no brown cone-like burr to compare with a gray wax berry; both species can be entire-margined, so 'teeth crowded at the very tip' is vacuous on an entire leaf; the leaves overlap in size (gale runs smaller, 2–5 ft shrub, but not reliably); and 'peat, not sand' is contradicted by the pond edges, damp swales and swamp margins this guide's own habitat text endorses. Its range runs across the northern tier into New England, New York and the Great Lakes and down the Pacific coast into Washington and Oregon, so it meets northern bayberry wherever a swale grades into peat and Pacific wax myrtle in the Northwest. THE CONSEQUENCE, WHICH IS WHAT YOU GET INSTEAD OF A RULE. Don't pick at the peat seam at all — the reason is not the ambiguity, it is that the same seam holds bog laurel and Labrador tea, which are graded deadly here, so 'I have found the aromatic bog shrub' resolves to at least three plants. And if one did get into a pot: sweet gale is a seasoning and beer-bittering herb in northern Europe, so this is not a poisoning emergency and not a reason to bin the pot on its own. It is a reason to keep that pot away from anyone pregnant or trying to conceive, because the plant is a listed abortifacient and contraindicated in pregnancy; its essential oil is toxic in quantity and the seed oil should never be ingested. Not poison. Not harmless either.

lookalikes.name: Camphor tree (Cinnamomum camphora)
lookalikes.tell: Aggressively naturalised through the Gulf and South Atlantic coastal plain and planted across coastal California, so a southeastern or western reader who gets camphor on a crush now has a plant to attach it to — line 5 rejects camphor in both halves of the range, not only on the West Coast. Its leaves are alternate, glossy, leathery, entire, 2–5 in, often tinged red when new, and the smell on a hard crush is unmistakable camphor. THE SPECIFIC TRAP: the underside carries DOMATIA, small swellings or pits in the vein axils, which a reader looking for resin dots can read as glands. They are not. There are two or three of them, sitting exactly where the main veins fork away from the midrib near the base, on a leaf with three prominent veins running from near the base — where Morella has one midrib with pinnate side veins and a scattered field of many small dots across the whole underside. It is also a large tree, to 60–100 ft, with a single trunk, not a multi-stemmed shrub. Camphor is absorbed readily and is a documented cause of seizures in children; the leaves are not food and do not belong in a pot in any quantity.

lookalikes.name: Heavenly bamboo (Nandina domestica)
lookalikes.tell: Ubiquitous in southeastern and West Coast foundation plantings, hedges and parking-lot beds, standing beside landscape wax myrtle, and it gets into a basket by a specific route: a DETACHED LEAFLET reads as a simple, entire, leathery, glossy 1–3 in leaf, pointed at both ends, often tinged red or bronze. Look at the plant, not the fragment. The leaf on the shrub is a large twice- or thrice-compound frond, with leaflets arranged along a jointed woody rachis, on erect unbranched cane-like stems. The leaflet has no resin dots and gives nothing on a hard crush. All parts are cyanogenic; the berries are toxic enough to have killed flocks of cedar waxwings that gorged on them, and the foliage is listed as poisonous to people and livestock. Nothing you pick from a foundation bed goes in a pot anyway — that is line 6.

lookalikes.name: Groundsel tree / eastern baccharis (Baccharis halimifolia) and coyote brush (B. pilularis)
lookalikes.tell: One genus, two coasts, the same wrong leaf. B. halimifolia shares northeastern and southeastern dune edges, marsh borders, fencerows and old fields at exactly bayberry's height, and in the Southeast the two grow into each other. B. pilularis is the dominant shrub of the California coastal scrub and bluff that this entry assigns to Morella californica — so a western reader meets this genus too, not just an eastern one. What works year-round on both, on leaf and twig: the leaves are thick and gray-green and obovate with only one to five large coarse teeth per side on the upper half; each leaf shows THREE prominent veins arising at or near the base, the composite-family trait, where bayberry has one midrib with pinnate side veins; and the underside carries no field of golden resin dots. The twigs are green and distinctly angled or ridged, where bayberry twigs are round, gray-brown and gland-dotted. Do not lean on the published autumn tell (fluffy white seed heads) — it is useless for most of the leaf-picking year and only ever works on female plants. Do not lean on 'Baccharis has no smell' either: both are resinous plants and a crushed leaf can smell faintly of turpentine or of very little. The honest statement is that neither ever smells of sweet balsam and candle wax. B. halimifolia carries cardioactive glycosides, has killed cattle and sheep, and is handled as a poisonous weed by Alabama Extension. B. pilularis is not documented as a human poison to anything like the same degree — it is mostly a nuisance and an allergen — but it is not food, and it will give a pot nothing but bitter resin.

lookalikes.name: Hollies and privet — yaupon (Ilex vomitoria), inkberry (I. glabra), myrtle-leaved holly (I. myrtifolia) and naturalised privet (Ligustrum sinense, L. japonicum)
lookalikes.tell: The other small-leaved leathery evergreens of southeastern thickets, hedgerows and dune scrub, and by sheer abundance the most likely wrong leaf to end up in your hand. None has resin dots and none gives you anything on a hard crush — lines 2 and 5 decide it before anything else. Beyond that: privet is opposite-leaved with small blunt entire leaves; yaupon is alternate but its leaves are only 0.5–1.5 in, rounded at the tip, with even rounded crenate teeth right around the margin, on stiff whitish-gray twigs; inkberry's are longer with a few teeth near the tip only; and myrtle-leaved holly — named for the resemblance, and sharing the pond-pine flatwoods, cypress pond margins and wet savannas that wax myrtle rims — has narrow stiff leaves under an inch with a sharp spine at the tip. Fruit settles it too: shiny red (yaupon, I. myrtifolia), black (inkberry, privet), never the bumpy gray-white wax ball. Holly berries and foliage cause vomiting, diarrhoea and abdominal pain; privet berries and foliage are rated toxic to people and livestock. Yaupon leaves do make a legitimate caffeinated tea, the one native North American caffeine plant, but they are not a bay leaf and contribute nothing to a pot except tannin.

lookalikes.name: Poison ivy and poison oak (Toxicodendron radicans, T. diversilobum)
lookalikes.tell: Listed here because it is a POT hazard, not only a skin one. Poison ivy grows as a shrub through northeastern bayberry stands and climbs up through them, and poison oak does the same on the West Coast, so you are reaching blind into exactly the height band they occupy. The leaf is COMPOUND — three leaflets on a common stalk, the middle one on a longer stalklet — but a single leaflet that has come away in your hand reads as a simple ovate leaf with a few irregular teeth, alternate on the twig, sometimes glossy. It has no resin dots, no sunken glands, and none of the bayberry smell, which is why line 2 and line 5 catch it — but only if you look at the leaf you actually picked rather than at the branch you picked it from. URUSHIOL IS NOT DESTROYED BY HEAT OR BY DRYING. It survives a drying screen, months in a jar, and a simmer, so a leaflet boiled in a stock puts urushiol into the food and into the steam, and the resulting reaction can involve the mouth, throat and gut rather than just the hands. Never burn the clippings either — the smoke carries it into the airway and that is a medical emergency. If a leaflet went in, the pot goes out.

lookalikes.name: Odorless bayberry (Morella inodora)
lookalikes.tell: Same genus, same gray waxy fruit, same wetlands — and no scent whatsoever, which is the entire point of listing it. It grows in acid streamhead bogs, bayheads, pond edges and stream banks along the northern Gulf: the Florida panhandle, southernmost Alabama and Mississippi, eastern Louisiana and southwestern Georgia — which is also Illicium ground, so this is a place where a scentless Morella and a strongly anise-scented non-Morella stand in the same bay swamp. Its leaves are thicker and larger than wax myrtle's, to 5 in, glossy, ovate to elliptic and entire, and crushing one gives you nothing at all. It will not hurt you, but it is the reason line 5 has to be run on every leaf you pick rather than once per bush: you confirm a bayberry by smelling the bayberry smell on that particular leaf, not by reasoning that the shrub is a Morella and therefore fine. It is also uncommon and of conservation concern across parts of its small range — leave it standing.

lookalikes.name: California bay laurel / pepperwood (Umbellularia californica)
lookalikes.tell: A West Coast problem, and not a poisoning risk — but it shares Pacific wax myrtle's coastal canyons and bluff slopes, it is powerfully aromatic, and it gets picked by mistake and then used in bayberry quantities. It is a tree, to 80 ft, with much larger leaves (2–5 in), smooth-margined and willow-like, no resin dots, and a sharp camphor-and-eucalyptus punch nothing like bayberry's sweet resin — which is why line 5 rejects camphor as firmly as it rejects almond and anise. It is safe to cook with in small amounts and is in fact the far stronger seasoning, one leaf where you would use four of bayberry, but a bayberry-sized dose turns a dish bitter and medicinal, and deeply inhaling a freshly crushed leaf gives some people an immediate violent headache — which is where the name 'headache tree' came from.

entry.harvest:
PICK ONE LEAF AT A TIME, and look at each one as it comes off. Never run a closed hand down a stem and never strip a branch into a bag — that is how a laurel, cherry, Illicium, Pieris or poison ivy leaf arrives without anyone having decided to pick it, and once leaves are dried and mixed the evidence of what went in is gone while every hazard here is still fully potent. Spread the picking in a single layer and run the six-line check again on every leaf before it goes into a jar. Take a few leaves from many shrubs rather than stripping one stem, and pick from the outside of the thicket: these are slow-growing dune and pocosin stabilisers, and on a northeastern back dune a bayberry thicket is often the only woody cover there is.

PICK THE NORTHEAST IN LEAF, ROUGHLY JUNE THROUGH SEPTEMBER — the only window this guide lists the species in at all, because from about November to April northern bayberry is bare or nearly so while every deadly evergreen here is in full glossy leaf. But that gate is for the Northeast. In the Southeast, South Central and West the deadly lookalikes are evergreen and just as present in July as in January, and southern and Pacific wax myrtle are pickable year-round in their own ranges. The calendar is not doing safety work for you outside the Northeast.

STAY ON GROUND THAT DRAINS, AND OFF THE PEAT SEAM. Where a swale or pond edge softens into saturated peat you are among sweet gale, bog laurel and Labrador tea, and the aromatic shrub standing with its feet in water is not worth the argument — walk back onto firm sand and pick there.

LEAVE THE FRUIT, whatever you are doing with the leaves. The gray wax drupes are one of the very few winter fat sources on the northeastern coast a bird can actually digest — the yellow-rumped warbler is among the only vertebrates able to break down the wax, which is what lets it winter further north than any other warbler, and staging tree swallows lean on the same fruit. Ignore the standard advice to take leaves from male plants: they are dioecious, but you cannot reliably sex one outside flower or fruit, and a handful of leaves costs a female shrub very little.

CHECK THE RULES FIRST, because this species grows disproportionately on protected ground. Collecting plants or plant parts is prohibited in National Park Service units under 36 CFR 2.1 — Cape Cod, Assateague, Cape Hatteras, Cape Lookout, Canaveral, Gulf Islands and Padre Island national seashores among them — and needs a permit on most National Wildlife Refuges. Dune vegetation is separately protected in most Atlantic coastal states and many beach towns: stay off the primary dune and out of fenced restoration plots and shorebird nesting areas entirely.

TWO HAZARDS INSIDE THE THICKET. Poison ivy grows through northeastern bayberry stands and poison oak does the same in the West, at exactly the height you will be reaching — look before you put a hand in, and never crush a doubtful leaf to smell it before you have looked at it. Urushiol is not destroyed by drying or by cooking, so a leaflet that comes home in the bag is a problem in the pot as well as on your skin, and burning the clippings puts it in your airway. These thickets also carry a heavy tick load right through the harvest season.

FINALLY, DO NOT PICK FROM ROADSIDE VERGES, MEDIANS, FOUNDATION BEDS OR CLIPPED HEDGES. That is where most of the accessible wax myrtle in the Southeast and on the West Coast actually is, it is routinely sprayed, and it is precisely where it stands shoulder to shoulder with oleander, cherry laurel, Florida anise, Pieris, Nandina and jessamine — planted for the same reasons, often in the same row. That is line 6, and it is the cheapest rejection in the entry.

blocking: The single 'pass' combination in `parts` is satisfied by a plant this entry itself grades toxic. The rule reads: sweet balsam and candle wax, alternate, sunken golden resin dots on a flat green underside, no latex, no petiole glands, no intramarginal vein, multi-stemmed shrub — 'that is the only combination that goes in the pot.' Myrica gale passes every clause of that: it is alternate, genuinely resin-dotted (same family), aromatic, latex-free, gland-free, vein-free and multi-stemmed. The entry separates sweet gale correctly in its lookalike tell (by ground and by fruit, never by smell) but never carries those disqualifiers back into the decision rule a reader will actually run. Since sweet gale is a listed abortifacient contraindicated in pregnancy, the gap has a real consequence. Fix is one clause: add to the pass line 'on ground that drains rather than saturated peat or standing water, with teeth not confined to the very tip of the leaf, and bearing round gray wax berries rather than a brown cone-like burr.'

months is [0..11] while regions includes 'northeast', and forageFor() in /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/data/foraging.ts filters strictly on region x month — so /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/components/ForageSection.tsx will list this under 'Coast & salt marsh' for a Northeast user in January and count it in 'N to look for in January'. That is precisely the window the entry's own harvest text calls the most dangerous: 'A leathery evergreen leaf taken off a northeastern dune thicket in January is more likely to be one of them than bayberry.' The warning exists only in `harvest`, which renders under 'Leave enough' after five paragraphs of `parts`; neither the collapsed row nor `habitat` nor `parts` carries any seasonal cue, so a partial reader gets a green light for the one scenario where the target plant is absent and every deadly lookalike is in full glossy leaf. The union-of-regions months convention used elsewhere in the corpus (e.g. Golden Chanterelle's winter months) is harmless there because an out-of-season listing just yields nothing; here it schedules the failure. Fix either way: trim months to the northern in-leaf window (roughly [4,5,6,7,8,9]) and state the southern/Pacific year-round availability in prose, or lead `habitat` with the June–September Northeast sentence so it appears in the collapsed row's lead and cannot be skipped.

MISSING DEADLY LOOKALIKE: the deciduous cyanogenic Prunus of the summer thicket. Chokecherry (P. virginiana) is a multi-stemmed shrub whose leaves are alternate, simple and obovate — widest above the middle, which is the exact leaf shape this entry gives for bayberry. Black cherry (P. serotina) and beach plum (P. maritima) are named BY THIS ENTRY as bayberry's own thicket companions in the habitat paragraph, and then appear nowhere in the lookalike list. All three carry prunasin and amygdalin, all three are most hazardous wilted or dried — which is precisely what this entry instructs (10-14 days in a paper bag, then a 20-30 minute simmer), and all three are in full leaf exactly in months 5-8, the only window the entry lists. The entry's entire seasonal safety argument is constructed around evergreens ('every deadly evergreen on the lookalike list stands in full glossy leaf' in winter) and never once acknowledges that the summer window it prescribes is the one season the deciduous Prunus are present in the same thicket. The three Prunus-tier entries it does carry are all evergreen and all described as glossy, thick, spine-toothed or tree-formed, so a reader has no tell that the soft deciduous shrub at their elbow in July is the same chemistry. Add them, with the petiole-gland and almond-crush tells the entry already teaches.

THE PASS RULE ADMITS SWEET GALE, WHICH THIS ENTRY ITSELF GRADES TOXIC AND CALLS AN ABORTIFACIENT CONTRAINDICATED IN PREGNANCY. The entry states outright that three clauses and only three clauses exclude Myrica gale, and all three can be unavailable at once. (a) Fruit: the clause is written conditionally — 'if the shrub is in fruit' — and the harvest section says the plants are dioecious and cannot be sexed outside flower or fruit, so on a male shrub the clause simply does not fire. (b) Teeth: the parts section says northern bayberry is 'usually entire', which makes 'any teeth spread along the upper half' vacuously true on an entire leaf and therefore a free pass. (c) Ground: 'sand that drains, not saturated peat' is contradicted by the entry's own habitat text, which places bayberry on 'pond and bog edges', 'damp swales', 'the upland margins of salt marshes', 'swamp margins' and 'pocosin and bay-forest rims', and by a terrain array that includes wetland. A beginner standing at a pond edge — habitat this entry endorses — holding an aromatic, alternate, resin-dotted, entire, fruitless leaf from a multi-stemmed shrub gets a clean PASS on sweet gale. The entry openly says these three clauses 'are the whole of what keeps it out of the pot', which is exactly the problem.

THE DEADLY GRAYANOTOXIN GROUP IS AN ENUMERATED SPECIES CHECKLIST WITH THE WEST COAST MISSING AND PIERIS MISSING. 'west' is a listed region, but every species in that lookalike is eastern except western Labrador tea. Rhododendron macrophyllum — the dominant leathery evergreen shrub of the coastal Pacific Northwest fog belt, squarely inside Morella californica's stated range of coastal bluffs, canyon bottoms and moist wooded slopes — is absent, as are Kalmia microphylla and Leucothoe davisiae. Separately, Pieris is absent in both halves of the range: P. japonica is among the most heavily planted leathery evergreen hedge shrubs in the Northeast and Southeast and stands in precisely the clipped-hedge exposure this entry names as its main practical risk, and P. phillyreifolia is native to southeastern bays and pocosins. The entry's own cited source (Jansen et al. 2012) names Pieris alongside Kalmia, so the reference is in the bibliography while the plant is not in the list. Because this group is written as a named roll-call rather than a rule, a reader will treat absence from it as absence from the thicket.
reasons: SCHEMA IS CLEAN. months [5,6,7,8] is correctly 0-indexed to June-September and matches the prose; regions, terrain, caution 'expert' and all eleven danger values are legal; no 'harmless' key; lookalikes all carry name/danger/tell. The month x region filter is conservative rather than over-broad: it restricts the evergreen-species regions to the northeastern-safe window rather than the other way round, so no reader is scheduled into a month when the target is absent.

The entry is genuinely strong where it is strong: the 'the pot is the dose, removing the leaf is not a safety step' thesis is correct and is the single most important thing to say about a bay-leaf substitute; the correction of the leaf-arrangement tell for Kalmia latifolia and Leucothoe axillaris is right and well sourced; specific durations and quantities (20-30 min simmer, 10-14 day dry, two leaves for one) are present; Poison Control number given. None of that is in dispute below.

Gelsemium sempervirens (Carolina jessamine) is unlisted. It is deadly, evergreen, leathery and it drapes through exactly the southeastern fencerows, hedges and roadside thickets the entry names as where most accessible wax myrtle actually stands. It gives nothing on a crush so the rejection rule catches it, but a reader working the lookalike list finds no entry for it.

Baccharis is covered for the East only. B. halimifolia is described in dune-edge/marsh-border/old-field terms; B. pilularis (coyote brush) is the dominant co-occurring shrub of the California coastal scrub and bluff that the entry assigns to Morella californica, is likewise resinous and likewise handled as toxic. A western reader gets the eastern species and eastern habitat.

Cinnamomum camphora is unlisted. It is aggressively naturalised through the Gulf and South Atlantic coastal plain, leathery, glossy, alternate and strongly aromatic. The crush rule rejects camphor, but attributes camphor solely to a West Coast tree, so a southeastern reader who gets camphor has no listed plant to attach it to.

Nandina domestica is unlisted and is ubiquitous in southeastern foundation plantings beside landscape wax myrtle. It is cyanogenic, and a detached leaflet reads as a simple, entire, leathery, glossy 1-3 in leaf.
Ilex myrtifolia (myrtle-leaved holly) is absent from the holly group despite being named for the resemblance and occupying the same pond-pine flatwoods ground as wax myrtle.

INTERNAL CONTRADICTION IN THE PASS RULE. The parts section describes northern bayberry as 'usually entire or carries a few blunt teeth on the upper third'; the pass rule requires 'any teeth spread along the upper half of the leaf rather than confined to the very tip'. A genuine northern bayberry leaf with teeth on the upper third fails the entry's own rule, and the rule's bayberry/sweet gale distinction ('upper third' vs 'confined to the very end') is finer than any beginner can operate in the field.

'WILTED OR DRIED LEAVES RELEASE MORE FREE CYANIDE THAN FRESH ONES' is correct for wilted Prunus foliage but overstated for fully dried material, which loses HCN over time. It errs safe and I would not block on it, but it is stated as flat fact in two lookalike entries.

The oleander cooking-skewer deaths are presented as documented. The tea and direct-ingestion fatalities are solid; the hot-dog-skewer story is widely treated as unverified. Soften or drop it — the heat-stable, water-soluble point stands on the tea cases alone.

USABILITY AT THE STATED AUDIENCE. The operative pass rule is a single nine-clause conjunctive sentence buried in an entry of roughly eight thousand words. 'expert' is the right caution value, but the entry is written for a reader who will read every word once and then work from memory in a tick-heavy thicket with poison ivy at arm height. The pass rule needs to be a numbered checklist that is short enough to be run leaf by leaf, as the entry itself demands.

The season gate does nothing for three of the four listed regions. In the southeast, southcentral and west every deadly lookalike here is evergreen and fully present in June-September. Worth saying plainly so readers there do not read the month restriction as a safety window that has been applied on their behalf.

Poison ivy and poison oak are flagged as a contact hazard while reaching, but the entry never says urushiol survives cooking and that a leaflet in the pot is itself a hazard — an odd omission in an entry whose central claim is that the pot, not the leaf, is the dose.

blocking: MISSING SERIOUSLY TOXIC LOOKALIKE — poison sumac (Toxicodendron vernix). This entry sends the reader to 'pond and bog edges', 'the damp swales behind the primary dune', 'the upland margins of salt marshes', 'pond and swamp margins, pocosin rims' and 'wet prairies'. That is poison sumac's exact habitat, and the guide already treats it as a mandatory lookalike in every other entry that touches that ground (elderberry line ~1123, staghorn sumac line ~2522, highbush blueberry line ~2775, and a warning in the spicebush harvest text). Its omission here is worse than an oversight because this entry builds an explicit DETACHED-LEAFLET argument for poison ivy and for Nandina — and poison sumac's leaflets are the ones that actually read as a bayberry leaf: 7-13 leaflets that are ENTIRE (untoothed), glossy, 2-4 in, alternate on the rachis, on a shrub-to-small-tree of exactly this height, where poison ivy's leaflets are irregularly toothed and trifoliolate. It carries urushiol at higher concentration than poison ivy, NC State rates it high severity, and this entry's own thesis is that urushiol survives drying and simmering and gets into the broth. A reader who knows only 'poison ivy has three leaflets' has no name for the entire-leafleted shrub standing in the swale. Add it as its own lookalike (danger 'toxic', matching the guide's grading of poison ivy) with the entire-margin / red rachis / lenticelled grey bark / drooping axillary whitish drupes tells, and name it in the harvest section's 'two hazards inside the thicket' paragraph, which currently names only poison ivy and poison oak.

MISSING SERIOUSLY TOXIC LOOKALIKE — ngaio, Myoporum laetum, on the West Coast, and it is the one plant that defeats this entry's single confirmatory character. Every other lookalike here is rejected by line 2 because it has no gland dots. Myoporum does: alternate, simple, leathery, glossy evergreen leaves 2-4 in, lanceolate, finely serrate in the upper half (i.e. matching this entry's own description of Pacific wax myrtle), with a conspicuous field of glandular dots visible held to the light. It is planted by the mile as a coastal windbreak and hedge in California and is naturalised on coastal bluffs, dune scrub and canyon mouths from the Bay Area south — Cal-IPC-listed, and precisely the ground this entry assigns to Morella californica. It is hepatotoxic (ngaione and related furanosesquiterpenoids), with well-documented fatal liver necrosis in cattle in New Zealand and California, and it is listed as toxic to humans. Run it through the six lines: line 1 passes (alternate, no latex), line 2 passes on a beginner's reading (a field of small dots in the blade), line 3 passes (no petiole glands), line 4 passes (stiff and leathery), line 6 passes on a naturalised bluff plant, and only line 5 is left — and line 5 names almond, anise, camphor, eucalyptus, turpentine and nothing, none of which is what a beginner will call ngaio. A hepatotoxin resting on one unnamed smell is not enough. It needs its own lookalike entry (translucent pellucid oil dots seen THROUGH the blade versus Morella's opaque sunken golden-orange glands that are gritty under a thumbnail; sticky varnished buds; a tree-like single trunk to 30 ft) and its scent added by name to line 5.

THE DECISION RULE ADMITS A PLANT THIS ENTRY ITSELF GRADES 'toxic', AND THE MITIGATION DOES NOT HOLD. The entry states outright that sweet gale (Myrica gale, danger 'toxic') clears lines 1-5, and offers line 6 — the peat seam — as the operative rejection. But line 6 rejects only 'peat that squelches, standing water'. Myrica gale is not confined to squelching peat: it holds firm sandy and gravelly lake shores, pond margins, stream banks and shoreline swales throughout the Northeast, the Great Lakes and the Pacific Northwest — which is ground line 6 explicitly permits and the habitat and indicator text actively sends the reader to ('pond and bog edges', 'the damp swales behind the primary dune'). So the entry's honest admission ('on a fruitless shrub at a pond edge in July there may be nothing in your hand that tells the two apart') is followed by a rule that does not in fact cover the case it just described. The entry cannot resolve this by adding a leaf clause — it is right that no leaf clause works — so it has to resolve it on the harvest side: restrict picking to dry back-dune, pine-barren, sandhill and old-field bayberry on ground that is dry at the surface, and strike pond edges, swale bottoms, bog margins, salt-marsh rims and pocosin rims from the habitat and indicator text as PICKING ground rather than leaving them there as places to look. As it stands, a reader following the habitat paragraph is picking in the exact zone the check cannot settle, and the stated consequence of the failure is a pot that must be kept from anyone pregnant.
reasons: Schema is clean: caution 'expert' is correct and required (multiple deadly lookalikes); every lookalikes[].danger is one of deadly/toxic/unpalatable with no illegal 'harmless'; terrain values are all legal Terrain members; regions are all legal RegionId values; months [5,6,7,8] is correctly 0-indexed to June-September and matches the prose window exactly, which is the failure this file most often shows and this entry gets right.

months x regions does not schedule anyone into an empty window. June-September is the correct northeastern leaf window, and southern/Pacific wax myrtle are evergreen and present throughout, so the shared array under-lists the South and West rather than misdirecting them — conservative, not dangerous. The entry is also explicitly right, and unusually clear, that the month gate protects the Northeast only and does nothing in the Southeast, South Central or West, where every deadly lookalike is evergreen.

The strongest material in the entry is the 'pot is the dose' paragraph and the refusal to treat lifting the leaf out as a safety step. That argument is correct for every toxin class named (cyanogenic glycosides surviving as the intact glycoside in the stock, heat-stable water-soluble cardiac glycosides and grayanotoxins, hot-water-extracted anisatin, urushiol surviving drying and heat), and the 'throw out the pot, not the leaf' instruction is the right operational conclusion. The Kalmia latifolia 'simple, alternate... occasionally opposite or whorled' correction and the refusal to let leaf arrangement clear the heath family are also correct and better than what most guides publish.

Internal grading inconsistency on sweet gale: the lookalike carries danger 'toxic' while its own tell ends 'Not poison. Not harmless either' and the parts text says a gale leaf in the pot 'is not a poisoning emergency and does not on its own mean throwing out the pot'. Pick one. The abortifacient and essential-oil cautions justify 'toxic'; the prose then argues against the grade the schema field asserts, and a reader scanning the danger badges gets a different message from the one the text intends.

Numeric inconsistency in the cherry laurel tell: 'Leaves run 1-2.5% cyanogenic glycosides, around 3.3 g prunasin equivalents per 100 g fresh' — 3.3 g/100 g is 3.3%, which sits outside the range stated in the same sentence. The cited source (Cicero et al.) carries both figures on different bases; say so or drop one, because as written it reads as an arithmetic error in the entry's most important lookalike.

Line 4 ('bend it') is the line the entry leans on hardest to separate the deciduous cherries and plums in summer, and it is weakest in the first month the entry lists. Northern bayberry leafs out in May, so a good deal of what is on the shrub in early June is still soft new growth; the entry's 'very new growth is soft on any shrub, take mature leaves' caveat is the right fix but it is one clause inside a long line, and a beginner who finds a soft leaf will reasonably conclude either 'not bayberry' or 'new growth, fine'. Worth restating line 4 as an instruction to work only on hardened current-season leaves from mid-June on.

Field memorability, which is the weakest structural thing here: the six-line check is buried in the middle of the `parts` field, after the culinary lede, the margins paragraph and the pot-is-the-dose paragraph. Given lead() shows only the first sentence of a field on a collapsed row, the reader's entry point to `parts` is 'The leaves, and only the leaves - used like a bay leaf', not the check. The six lines themselves are runnable from memory; what is not memorable is the exception structure wrapped around them — one lookalike the check cannot settle, a calendar rule that applies in one region and not the others, and a 'this rejects but never confirms' framing. Lead `parts` with the check.

One vague quantity in an entry that is otherwise specific (20-30 minute simmer, two leaves for one, 10-14 days drying, start with one leaf for Pacific wax myrtle): the sweet gale consequence says 'do not use in quantity' and 'do not make it a routine' with no number, in the one place where a reader has already been told the leaf may be undetectable.

Minor, consistent with house convention so not blocking: terrain includes 'wetland' and 'disturbed', which files this species under 'Streambank & wet ground' and 'Disturbed ground & yards' in forageByTerrain — the two grounds the harvest section forbids picking on. The blueberry and elderberry entries do the same thing, so this matches the file's practice, but here the disturbed-ground listing points at the clipped hedges and roadside verges the entry calls its single largest practical risk.

Two further unnamed neighbours that the check does reject, noted only so the next pass can decide: glossy buckthorn (Frangula alnus), a toxic invasive of exactly the northeastern swale and pond-margin seam, and naturalised eucalyptus on the California coast, whose leaves are gland-dotted and visible against the light. Both fail line 2 or line 5 as written, so neither is a blocker, but eucalyptus is named in line 5 by smell without ever being given a plant in the lookalike list, which leaves the reader rejecting a scent they cannot attach to anything.
